list-item.p: Venetoclax and R-GDP can be safely combined.
High efficacy is observed at the recommended phase 2 dose.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Although chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy has supplanted autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) for most patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 1 line of therapy, ASCT may still be a suitable therapy for some patients, especially those with late relapse. Rituximab, gemcitabine, dexamethasone and cisplatin (R-GDP) is an established salvage chemotherapy regimen used to induce responses before ASCT. LY.18 is a phase I platform study aimed at adding new agents to R-GDP to determine their safety and recommended phase 2 dose. The first arm of LY.18 tested escalating dose levels of venetoclax in combination with 3 cycles of R-GDP at standard doses. In total, 24 patients were treated. The main adverse events were hematologic symptoms, infection, gastrointestinal symptoms, and fatigue. Rates of febrile neutropenia improved after an amendment introducing mandatory granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. The recommended phase 2 dose of venetoclax was 400 mg on days 4 to 10 of cycle 1 and on days 1 to 10 of cycles 2 and 3. The overall response rate (ORR) was 70.8% (95% confidence interval, 51.5-86.9), and the complete response (CR) rate was 12.5%. In a post hoc comparison with a similar cohort of patients treated contemporaneously with R-GDP, there was no difference in the event-free and overall survival, although the ORR was numerically higher. R-GDP and venetoclax has a manageable safety profile and is effective, although further development of this regimen is unlikely because of the low CR rates observed and the advent of more effective therapies for treating in R/R LBCL. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT04161248.

sec.p: Received 2026 Jan 9; Accepted 2026 Mar 16; Collection date 2026 Aug.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Front-line therapies for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (BCL; DLBCL) achieve cure in ∼60% of patients.1,2 For those who experience early relapse or primary refractory disease, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can provide high rates of long-term remission.3,4 However, access to CAR T-cell treatment may be limited because of the costs, logistics, and availability globally.5,6 Salvage chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) remain the standard curative option for transplant-eligible patients who are unable to receive CAR T-cell therapy or in those who relapse later in their disease course.

However, only ∼25% of patients who are eligible for salvage therapy and ASCT ultimately achieve long-term remission through this approach.7,8 The main obstacle to achieving this goal is suboptimal response rates to salvage therapy, which remains a prerequisite for proceeding to the transplant. Approximately 45% to 55% of patients achieve a partial response (PR) or complete response (CR) to salvage therapy, and the rate is lower among patients with early relapse or primary refractory disease.7 ASCT itself leads to long-term remissions in ∼50% of patients.9

Improving the response to salvage chemotherapy by using different chemotherapy regimens has not led to greater efficacy.7,8 Consequently, therapeutic focus has shifted toward adding novel agents to salvage protocols with the aim of improving the response rates and enabling more patients to proceed to transplantation. The Canadian Cancer Trials Group LY.18 phase 1 platform study for patients with DLBCL after 1 previous line of therapy includes several nonrandomized arms. Here, we report the outcomes of cohort A in which the combination of venetoclax, an oral, small-molecule, selective BCL2 inhibitor, with rituximab, gemcitabine, dexamethasone, and cisplatin (R-GDP) was tested (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04161248). BCL2 promotes cell survival and chemoresistance by blocking apoptosis, and BCL2 overexpression is common in DLBCL, including in the high-risk double expressor and DLBCL with MYC and BCL2 rearrangement (double hit; DLBCL-DH-BCL2) groups. By targeting BCL2, venetoclax restores the apoptotic pathway and may increase chemosensitivity (reviewed in a study by Leverson et al10).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Eligible patients had relapsed or refractory DLBCL, including primary mediastinal LBCL, T-cell/histocyte-rich LBCL, high-grade BCL, and transformed, low-grade lymphoma, and had received 1 previous line of therapy for DLBCL. Patients with histologic transformation from follicular, marginal, and lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma could have received up to 3 previous lines of therapy for their indolent lymphoma.

Patients aged ≥16 years with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score of 0 to 3 must have been considered fit for intensive chemotherapy, have had radiologically measurable disease, and adequate hematologic, hepatic, and renal function. BCL2 expression was not an eligibility requirement but was recorded for all patients. The protocol in the supplemental Material, clinical trial protocol provides the full eligibility details.

R-GDP was given in 3-week cycles for up to 3 courses at standard doses.8 Venetoclax was administered from days 4 to 10 of cycle 1 and days 1 to 10 of cycles 2 and 3. Dose escalation was performed according to a 3+3 design with 3 dose levels, namely 200 mg at dose level 1, 400 mg at dose level 2, and 800 mg at dose level 3. A dose level −1, comprising 200 mg venetoclax daily on days 4 to 8 of cycle 1 and days 1 to 5 of cycles 2 and 3, was also included. The protocol was amended to include granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) prophylaxis from days 9 to 14 of each cycle when high rates of neutropenia were observed at dose level 1. An additional 6 patients were treated at the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). Response assessments were performed by positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan after 3 cycles of therapy, and peripheral blood stem cell mobilization assessments were conducted according to institutional standards.

The primary objective of this study was to establish the maximum tolerated dose and RP2D. Secondary objectives included the overall response rate (ORR) as determined by both the Lugano criteria11 and RECIL (Response Evaluation Criteria in Lymphoma).12 According to the protocol, all patients who received at least 1 cycle of therapy and had their disease re-evaluated were considered evaluable for response, along with those who exhibited objective disease progression before the end of cycle 1. Additional secondary endpoints included toxicity (using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.0 [CTCAE V4.0]), stem cell collection rate, transplantation rate, overall survival (OS), and event-free survival (EFS). EFS was defined as disease progression or discontinuation of treatment for any reason. In a post hoc analysis, the response rate and survival endpoints were compared with that of a contemporaneously enrolled cohort of patients who received R-GDP in the control arm of the LY.17 randomized phase 2 study, which enrolled in the same centers and had the same inclusion criteria as in LY.18.13 For the available tumor samples, assignment of the cell of origin by digital gene expression (DLBCL90)14 was performed.
Descriptive statistics were used for the baseline characteristics and outcomes. The Kaplan-Meier method and survival curves were used to estimate the survival outcomes.

All enrolled patients provided written informed consent. The study was approved by the research ethics board at each participating center. The trial was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, International Conference on Harmonization Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice, and appropriate laws and regulations.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: From 1 September 2020 to 1 August 2024, 24 patients were enrolled. The baseline patient characteristics are shown in Table 1. The median age was 59 years (range, 19-68), most patients were male, 17 patients had de novo tumors of LBCL morphology, and 7 had transformed follicular lymphoma. All patients previously had received RCHOP-like (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine, prednisone) chemotherapy, and all but 4 patients had high-risk disease with refractory disease or relapse within 1 year of therapy. In 20 patients, BCL2 expression was present, as measured by immunohistochemistry; in 4 patients, this was not reported. The cell-of-origin assignment was performed in biopsies from 13 patients with available material, using digital gene expression, with the assay failing in tumors from 3 patients. The standard cell of origin was germinal center B-cell–like in 8 patients and activated B-cell–like in 2 patients. The dark zone (DZ) signature was positive in 5 of the 8 germinal center B-cell tumors. Of 14 tumors tested, 5 were DLBCL-DH-BCL2. In total, 7 of the 19 tested patients had either DZ and/or DLBCL-DH-BCL2 tumors.

fn.p: ABC, activated B-cell–like; CCO, cell of origin; ECOG, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group; GCB, germinal center B-cell–like; TTP time to progression.

sec.p: Among the 3 patients treated at dose level 1, 2 experienced dose limiting neutropenia. As per the study design, 3 patients were then treated at dose level −1; concurrently, the protocol was amended to incorporate G-CSF prophylaxis at all dose levels. No dose limiting toxicities (DLTs) occurred at dose levels −1, 1 + G-CSF, and 2. At dose level 3, there were 2 DLTs, febrile neutropenia, and neutropenia. Dose level 2 was therefore chosen as the RP2D. The DLTs are detailed in Table 2. The median dose intensity for R-GDP was >97% for all agents, except dexamethasone (supplemental Table 1). Dose reductions or interruptions of venetoclax occurred in 2 patients at the RP2D. There were 10 serious adverse events, including febrile neutropenia (n = 4), infective phlebitis, bacteremia, fever, abdominal pain, fall, and supraventricular tachycardia. The adverse events that occurred in ≥10% patients are listed in Table 3. Grade 3/4 clinical adverse events were febrile neutropenia (n = 4), supraventricular tachycardia (n = 1), abdominal pain (n = 1), fatigue (n = 1), and infection (n = 5), including phlebitis, sepsis, and the urinary tract. The most common adverse events (occurring in ≥30% of patients) were cytopenia, infections, gastrointestinal complaints, fatigue, and biochemical abnormalities. Two patients experienced reversible grade 3 alanine aminotransferase and/or aspartate aminotransferase elevation. No patients had tumor lysis syndrome. There were 6 deaths, 5 owing to disease progression, and 1 owing to complications of ASCT; no deaths were attributed to therapy with venetoclax–R-GDP.

fn.p: RECIL, Response Evaluation Criteria in Lymphoma.

fn.p: ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; GERD, gastroesophageal reflux disease.

sec.p: Of the 24 treated patients, 17 completed therapy, 3 discontinued therapy because of disease progression, and 4 discontinued owing to adverse events. Three patients completed cycle 1 of venetoclax and R-GDP (1 experienced a serious adverse event, febrile neutropenia) but were taken off the study without a response assessment; 1 for infective phlebitis, 1 for prolonged grade 2 creatinine elevation and vestibular disorder considered possibly related to treatment, and the third for prolonged neutropenia related to treatment. A CONSORT diagram of patient disposition is provided in supplemental Figure 1. Among the 21 evaluable patients, the ORR based on the Lugano criteria11 was 81.0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 61.9-94.5) with 3 CRs, 14 PRs, 1 stable disease (SD), and 3 with progressive disease (PD). Based on RECIL criteria,12 the ORR was identical, although 4 patients were classified as having achieved CR, and 13 were classified as having PR. The ORR at the RP2D was 78% (95% CI, 46.8-97.3). The response rates by dose level are shown in Table 2. Among the 7 patients with either DLBCL-DH-BCL2 and/or DZ lymphoma, 5 had PR and 2 had PD.

Of the 24 treated patients, 16 had an attempted stem cell collection. In 13 of these patients, the collection met the protocol definition for success of ≥2 × 106 CD34+ cells per kg body weight (81.3%; 95% CI, 59.2-95.9). Overall, 14 of 24 patients underwent an ASCT (58.3%; 95% CI, 38.5-76.9).

The median duration of follow-up was 8.94 months (range, 2.83-29.08). The median EFS for all patients was 4.07 months (95% CI, 2.37-8.71), and the median OS was not reached, with an estimated 24-month OS of 66% (95% CI, 38-83). The Kaplan-Meier curves for EFS and OS are shown in Figures 1 and 2, respectively.

p.bold: Kaplan-Meier curve showing EFS for patients treated with venetoclax–R-GDP in the LY.18 phase I study.
Kaplan-Meier curve showing OS for patients treated with venetoclax–R-GDP the LY.18 phase 1 study.

sec.p: In a contemporaneously enrolled cohort that consisted of 35 patients who were treated with R-GDP in the Canadian Cancer Trials Group LY.17 phase 2 study, the ORR was 48.6% (2 CR, 15 PR, 5 SD, 11 PD; supplemental Table 2).13 Of these, 18 of 20 (90%) had a successful stem cell collection attempt, defined as ≥2 × 106 CD34+ cells per kg body weight. Nineteen of 35 patients (54.3%, including 3 patients with SD) underwent ASCT. The OS and EFS for this cohort are shown in supplemental Figure 2, superimposed on the primary LY.18 cohort results. The median survival following ASCT was not reached in either the LY.18 or LY.17 cohorts, and the outcomes were highly similar (supplemental Figure 3). With regards to toxicity, 3% of patients experienced febrile neutropenia and 29% had an infection in the R-GDP LY.17 cohort as opposed to 16.7% and 62.5%, respectively, among patients treated with R-GDP–venetoclax in LY.18. Furthermore, we compared the number of treatment cycle delays for adverse events. In total, there were 15 cycle delays due to adverse events in LY.18, specifically 2 for febrile neutropenia, 9 for neutropenia, 3 for thrombocytopenia, and 1 for rash. The average cycle delay length was 10.1 days (range, 6-22). For LY.17, there were 11 cycle delays owing to adverse events, including neutropenia in 5, thrombocytopenia in 1, and fever, chest pain, neuropathy, pneumonia, and hearing loss in 1 each. The average delay was 7.3 days (range, 3-14). Thus, more treatment delays owing to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia were observed among patients treated with R-GDP and venetoclax than with R-GDP alone.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: LY.18 is a phase 1 platform trial in which the combination of R-GDP and venetoclax was evaluated in 1 study arm. This combination proved to be tolerated and effective at the RP2D of 400 mg venetoclax on days 4 to 10 of cycle 1 and days 1 to 10 of cycles 2 and 3, although G-CSF prophylaxis was necessary to reduce febrile neutropenia. R-GDP could be given at the standard doses in most cases, and the addition of venetoclax did not impair stem cell collection. The main toxicities were hematologic and infectious, and the main DLT was febrile neutropenia. The response rate at the RP2D and for the cohort appeared to be higher than that observed with R-GDP alone. However, this did not appear to affect transplantation rates or survival.

The intention upon completion of this phase 1 study was to incorporate R-GDP and venetoclax at the RP2D into the LY.17 protocol, a randomized, phase 2 platform trial that evaluated novel agents plus R-GDP against R-GDP among transplant-eligible patients with relapsed DLBCL.15 Because of the emergence of CAR T-cell therapy as the superior therapeutic option over salvage chemotherapy and ASCT for patients with refractory or early relapsed DLBCL, LY.17 was closed and a formal randomized comparison of venetoclax plus R-GDP vs R-GDP alone is not planned.

CAR T-cell therapy is not available for all qualifying patients with DLBCL with a first relapse because of issues related to accessibility, cost, and logistics.5,6 Currently, CAR T-cell therapy is not approved for patients with relapses of DLBCL >1 year after treatment; in our cohort, this represented only a small proportion of patients (4/24). The ZUMA-7 and TRANSFORM trials that compared CAR T-cell therapies as second-line treatment with salvage chemotherapy and ASCT clearly demonstrated that patients who were able to receive an ASCT had favorable survival, paralleling that of patients who received CAR T-cell therapy.3,4 In these trials, patients who were randomized to salvage therapy and ASCT experienced early progression and a lack of response to salvage therapy, suggesting that an improvement in salvage treatment could allow for greater success of ASCT and improved OS. In this cohort of the LY.18 trial, R-GDP–venetoclax was associated with numerically higher ORRs when compared with R-GDP alone, but this did not translate into higher rates of ASCT. This may be because of the relatively low rates of CR in our study as positron emission tomography–negative CRs are associated with superior outcomes following ASCT.16 The low CR rates in our study can be explained by the high number of patients with primary refractory disease, and the high number of patients with DLBCL-DH-BCL2 and/or DZ lymphoma, 2 adverse prognostic factors associated with resistance to chemoimmunotherapy.17 A larger sample size would be needed to confirm these observations. In comparison with the LY.17 cohort, patients in this study had higher rates of febrile neutropenia and infection, reflecting the compounded myelosuppression associated with venetoclax. In addition, there were longer and more treatment delays with R-GDP–venetoclax than with R-GDP alone. Although the mobilization rate appeared to be lower in the venetoclax–R-GDP cohort than in the LY.17 cohort, a larger sample size is needed to determine if the addition of venetoclax impairs stem cell mobilization.

Other studies have examined the addition of novel agents to salvage chemotherapy in DLBCL. Venetoclax has been combined with R-ICE (rituximab, ifosfamide, carboplatin and etoposide), another common salvage regimen in DLBCL for patients who intend to undergo ASCT. The ORR was 81% in this trial, and 61% of patients proceeded to transplant; the 2-year progression-free survival and OS were 52% and 59%, respectively.18 Reasons for no transplant included failure to mobilize, patient preference, and treatment with CAR T-cell therapy. Another trial of R-ICE with ibrutinib also showed a very high response rate of 90%, CR of 55%, and an OS of 65% in 20 treated patients.19 In contrast, in the LY.17 trial that evaluated R-GDP–ibrutinib, we observed high rates of infection that led to early termination of this arm.15 More recent trials have examined the addition of anti-CD3/anti-CD20 bispecific antibodies to salvage chemotherapy. The combination of epcoritamab and R-ICE was associated with an ORR of 80%, CR of 65%, and a 60% transplantation rate.20 Glofitamab and R-ICE21 and epcoritamab R-DHAP/X (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine and cisplatin or oxaliplatin)22 are associated with similarly high CR rates and transplantation rates. R-GDP–glofitamab was also tested in the LY.18 study platform.23 The final results of this study are awaited. Overall, bispecific combinations appear to provide superior CR rates than that observed in our study.

It appears that once ASCT is administered, the long-term survival of patients is unaffected by the addition of the novel agent at the salvage chemotherapy stage based on our and other data. Whether this agent should be added to conditioning or as post-ASCT maintenance is a question likely to remain unanswered.

Although CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is a superior second-line therapy for refractory and early relapsed DLBCL, for patients who do not have access to or who do not qualify for this therapy and those with later relapse, refinement of salvage chemotherapy and ASCT should remain an important research goal. Enthusiasm for venetoclax plus chemotherapy for relapsed/refractory DLBCL has waned because of limited efficacy and safety concerns.24 Similarly, our study did not demonstrate improved outcomes. Emerging modalities, such as bispecific antibodies, hold greater promise in this clinical setting.
